Retract

/rih-TRAKT/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Retract means to take back a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong

Retract means to take back a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong. The newspaper had to retract its front-page report once documents proved the local factory had actually passed its safety inspection.

Worked Example

After an outside team found a critical error in the lab's measurements, the chemist chose to retract the paper rather than defend a flawed result.

Retract fits because the chemist is formally taking back a published claim — the paper — specifically because it was discovered to be wrong, which is the word's core situation in science and publishing.

How Retract Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

withdraw

withdraw: to pull back or take back something offered or stated

rescind

rescind: to officially cancel a decision, offer, or rule

recant

recant: to formally give up a belief or statement one once held

Antonyms

affirm

affirm: to state firmly that something is true

maintain

maintain: to continue insisting that a claim is correct

How Strong Is It? — qualify → abjure → retract

qualify vs. retract

qualify vs. retract: To qualify a statement is weaker — you soften it or add conditions while still standing behind it, instead of retracting it outright.

abjure vs. retract

abjure vs. retract: To abjure is stronger — it is a solemn, often sworn renouncing of a belief entirely, going beyond retracting one mistaken statement.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back (Latin)

Root — tract

Root — tract: to pull, to drag (Latin trahere, past participle tractus)

Put it together

Put it together: Retract is literally 'to pull back' — the same physical image behind a cat retracting its claws — and when applied to words, it means pulling a statement or claim back in after you have let it out.

Use the root in a new word: distract

Use the root in a new word: distract: The buzzing phone kept trying to distract Jonah, pulling his attention away from the practice test.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral–formal

Retract is the standard word in journalism, science, and law — newspapers retract stories, researchers retract papers, witnesses retract testimony. It also keeps its literal 'pull back' sense (a cat retracts its claws). In casual conversation, people usually say 'take back' instead.
